title: Remove Outermost Parentheses
notes:
Task and constraints: Remove the outermost pair of parentheses from every primitive valid-parentheses substring.
Idea: Track nesting depth and append an opening or closing parenthesis only when it is not the outermost character of a primitive group.
Technique and why it applies: Depth transitions reveal the outermost pair without needing to split the string into primitives first.
Invariant: Depth is the number of open parentheses before the current character; depth transitions identify each primitive's outer pair.
Edge cases: The input is a valid parentheses string; depth zero marks boundaries between primitive components; outermost characters are omitted.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(n) output space.
complexity_reason: Depth transitions reveal the outermost pair without needing to split the string into primitives first.

title: Remove Outermost Parentheses
notes:
Task and constraints: Remove the outermost pair of parentheses from every primitive valid-parentheses substring.

Technique and why it applies: Depth transitions reveal the outermost pair without needing to split the string into primitives first.
Invariant: Depth is the number of open parentheses before the current character; depth transitions identify each primitive's outer pair.
Edge cases: The input is a valid parentheses string; depth zero marks boundaries between primitive components; outermost characters are omitted.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(n) output space.
code: class Solution { public String removeOuterParentheses(String s){StringBuilder b=new StringBuilder();int depth=0;for(char c:s.toCharArray()){if(c=='('){if(depth>0)b.append(c);depth++;}else{depth--;if(depth>0)b.append(c);}}return b.toString();} }
complexity_reason: Depth transitions reveal the outermost pair without needing to split the string into primitives first.

title: Sum of Root To Leaf Binary Numbers
notes:
Task and constraints: Each root-to-leaf path encodes a binary number; return the sum of all such values.
Idea: During DFS, update the path value as `value*2 + node.val`; add that value only when a node is a leaf.
Technique and why it applies: Appending each node bit with a left shift and addition builds the root-to-leaf binary value directly.
Invariant: The parameter carried to each node is the binary value of the root-to-current-node path.
Edge cases: A single-node tree contributes its own bit; null children contribute nothing; tree values are binary digits.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(h) recursion space.
complexity_reason: Appending each node bit with a left shift and addition builds the root-to-leaf binary value directly.

title: Sum of Root To Leaf Binary Numbers
notes:
Task and constraints: Each root-to-leaf path encodes a binary number; return the sum of all such values.
Idea: During DFS, update the path value as `value*2 + node.val`; add that value only when a node is a leaf.
Technique and why it applies: Appending each node bit with a left shift and addition builds the root-to-leaf binary value directly.
Invariant: The parameter carried to each node is the binary value of the root-to-current-node path.
Edge cases: A single-node tree contributes its own bit; null children contribute nothing; tree values are binary digits.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(h) recursion space.
code: class Solution { public int sumRootToLeaf(TreeNode root){return dfs(root,0);}private int dfs(TreeNode n,int v){if(n==null)return 0;v=v*2+n.val;if(n.left==null&&n.right==null)return v;return dfs(n.left,v)+dfs(n.right,v);} }
complexity_reason: Appending each node bit with a left shift and addition builds the root-to-leaf binary value directly.

title: Divisor Game
notes:
Task and constraints: Return true if Alice wins the divisor game starting from n, where players subtract a proper divisor and n=1 loses.
Idea: Return whether `n` is even; under optimal play, every even state can move to an odd state and every odd state leaves the opponent an even state.
Technique and why it applies: The parity strategy proves even starting values win and odd starting values lose under optimal play.
Invariant: The winning state alternates with parity: one is losing, and choosing divisor one flips parity for every state above one.
Edge cases: For n=1 return false; n is positive; no simulation of all divisors is needed.
Complexity: O(1) time and O(1) space.
code:
class Solution:
 def divisorGame(self,n):return n%2==0
complexity_reason: The parity strategy proves even starting values win and odd starting values lose under optimal play.

title: Matrix Cells in Distance Order
notes:
Task and constraints: Return all matrix coordinates ordered by Manhattan distance from (r0,c0), breaking ties by row and then column.
Idea: Enumerate every `(r,c)` coordinate and sort by Manhattan distance `abs(r-r0)+abs(c-c0)`, then by row and column for ties.
Technique and why it applies: Sorting by the complete distance-and-coordinate key enforces both the primary order and tie-breaking rules.
Invariant: The sorted coordinate list is ordered by the exact tuple `(distance,row,column)` required by the problem.
Edge cases: The origin is included; ties require deterministic row-then-column ordering; all matrix coordinates appear exactly once.
Complexity: O(mn log(mn)) time and O(mn) space.
complexity_reason: Sorting by the complete distance-and-coordinate key enforces both the primary order and tie-breaking rules.

title: Matrix Cells in Distance Order
notes:
Task and constraints: Return all matrix coordinates ordered by Manhattan distance from (r0,c0), breaking ties by row and then column.
Idea: Enumerate every `(r,c)` coordinate and sort by Manhattan distance `abs(r-r0)+abs(c-c0)`, then by row and column for ties.
Technique and why it applies: Sorting by the complete distance-and-coordinate key enforces both the primary order and tie-breaking rules.
Invariant: The sorted coordinate list is ordered by the exact tuple `(distance,row,column)` required by the problem.
Edge cases: The origin is included; ties require deterministic row-then-column ordering; all matrix coordinates appear exactly once.
Complexity: O(mn log(mn)) time and O(mn) space.
code:
import java.util.*;
class Solution { public int[][] allCellsDistOrder(int rows,int cols,int rCenter,int cCenter){List<int[]>a=new ArrayList<>();for(int r=0;r<rows;r++)for(int c=0;c<cols;c++)a.add(new int[]{r,c});a.sort((x,y)->{int d=Math.abs(x[0]-rCenter)+Math.abs(x[1]-cCenter),e=Math.abs(y[0]-rCenter)+Math.abs(y[1]-cCenter);if(d!=e)return d-e;if(x[0]!=y[0])return x[0]-y[0];return x[1]-y[1];});return a.toArray(new int[0][]);} }
complexity_reason: Sorting by the complete distance-and-coordinate key enforces both the primary order and tie-breaking rules.

title: Valid Boomerang
notes:
Task and constraints: Return true if three distinct points are not collinear.
Idea: Compute the cross product of vectors from the first point to the other two and return true exactly when it is nonzero.
Technique and why it applies: The cross product tests collinearity directly without dividing or handling vertical-line slopes.
Invariant: A zero cross product means the two vectors are parallel and the three points are collinear.
Edge cases: Repeated points also produce zero cross product; integer arithmetic avoids floating-point slope errors.
Complexity: O(1) time and O(1) space.
complexity_reason: The cross product tests collinearity directly without dividing or handling vertical-line slopes.

title: Valid Boomerang
notes:
Task and constraints: Return true if three distinct points are not collinear.
Idea: Compute the cross product of vectors from the first point to the other two and return true exactly when it is nonzero.
Technique and why it applies: `isBoomerang` compares `(p[1][0]-p[0][0])*(p[2][1]-p[0][1])` with `(p[1][1]-p[0][1])*(p[2][0]-p[0][0])`; unequal products mean the three points are not collinear.
Invariant: A zero cross product means the two vectors are parallel and the three points are collinear.
Edge cases: Repeated points also produce zero cross product; integer arithmetic avoids floating-point slope errors.
Complexity: O(1) time and O(1) space.
code: class Solution { public boolean isBoomerang(int[][] p){return (p[1][0]-p[0][0])*(p[2][1]-p[0][1])!=(p[1][1]-p[0][1])*(p[2][0]-p[0][0]);} }
complexity_reason: The two products of coordinate differences in `p` detect collinearity without slope division.

title: Last Stone Weight
approach_name: Repeatedly smash the two heaviest stones
notes:
Task and constraints: Repeatedly remove the two heaviest stones; if their weights differ, put the difference back. Return the final weight or zero.
Idea: Store stone weights in a max-heap, repeatedly remove the two largest, and reinsert their positive difference when they differ.
Technique and why it applies: A max-heap retrieves the two heaviest stones efficiently for every smash.
Invariant: The heap always contains the weights of all stones remaining after completed smash operations.
Edge cases: Fewer than two stones ends the process; equal weights remove both; an empty heap returns zero.
Complexity: O(n log n) time and O(n) space.
complexity_reason: A max-heap retrieves the two heaviest stones efficiently for every smash.

title: Last Stone Weight
approach_name: Repeatedly smash the two heaviest stones
notes:
Task and constraints: Repeatedly remove the two heaviest stones; if their weights differ, put the difference back. Return the final weight or zero.
Idea: Store stone weights in a max-heap, repeatedly remove the two largest, and reinsert their positive difference when they differ.
Technique and why it applies: A max-heap retrieves the two heaviest stones efficiently for every smash.
Invariant: The heap always contains the weights of all stones remaining after completed smash operations.
Edge cases: Fewer than two stones ends the process; equal weights remove both; an empty heap returns zero.
Complexity: O(n log n) time and O(n) space.
code:
import java.util.*;
class Solution { public int lastStoneWeight(int[] stones){PriorityQueue<Integer>q=new PriorityQueue<>(Collections.reverseOrder());for(int x:stones)q.add(x);while(q.size()>1){int a=q.remove(),b=q.remove();if(a!=b)q.add(a-b);}return q.isEmpty()?0:q.remove();} }
complexity_reason: A max-heap retrieves the two heaviest stones efficiently for every smash.

title: Remove All Adjacent Duplicates In String
notes:
Task and constraints: Repeatedly remove adjacent equal character pairs until no such pair remains.
Idea: Use a stack: if the next character equals the stack top, pop it; otherwise push the character.
Technique and why it applies: Stack popping handles both immediate duplicates and cascading pairs revealed by earlier removals.
Invariant: The stack represents the reduced prefix after all adjacent equal pairs have been removed, so popping can expose a new pair for later characters.
Edge cases: Cascading removals are handled naturally; an empty stack accepts any character; the final stack is the remaining string.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(n) space.
complexity_reason: Stack popping handles both immediate duplicates and cascading pairs revealed by earlier removals.

title: Remove All Adjacent Duplicates In String
notes:

Technique and why it applies: Stack popping handles both immediate duplicates and cascading pairs revealed by earlier removals.
Invariant: The stack represents the reduced prefix after all adjacent equal pairs have been removed, so popping can expose a new pair for later characters.
Edge cases: Cascading removals are handled naturally; an empty stack accepts any character; the final stack is the remaining string.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(n) space.
code: class Solution { public String removeDuplicates(String s){StringBuilder b=new StringBuilder();for(char c:s.toCharArray()){int n=b.length();if(n>0&&b.charAt(n-1)==c)b.deleteCharAt(n-1);else b.append(c);}return b.toString();} }
complexity_reason: Stack popping handles both immediate duplicates and cascading pairs revealed by earlier removals.

title: Height Checker
notes:
Task and constraints: Return the number of indices where the original height array differs from its sorted version.
Idea: Sort a copy of the heights and count indices where the original value differs from the sorted value.
Technique and why it applies: Comparing original positions against a sorted copy counts exactly the positions that need reordering.
Invariant: The sorted copy is the target nondecreasing order, and each mismatch is exactly a student whose position differs from expected.
Edge cases: Duplicate heights are allowed; the original array must remain available for comparison.
Complexity: O(n log n) time and O(n) space for the sorted copy.
complexity_reason: Comparing original positions against a sorted copy counts exactly the positions that need reordering.

code:
import java.util.*;
class Solution { public int heightChecker(int[] heights){int[]a=heights.clone();Arrays.sort(a);int n=0;for(int i=0;i<a.length;i++)if(a[i]!=heights[i])n++;return n;} }
complexity_reason: Comparing original positions against a sorted copy counts exactly the positions that need reordering.

title: Greatest Common Divisor of Strings
notes:
Task and constraints: Return the longest string that divides both input strings by repetition, or an empty string if none exists.
Idea: If `str1+str2` differs from `str2+str1`, return empty; otherwise the common repeating base has length `gcd(len(str1),len(str2))`.
Technique and why it applies: Cross-concatenation equality tests a shared repeating pattern, while the length GCD selects its longest base.
Invariant: Concatenation equality establishes that both strings are repetitions of the same base, and the length GCD gives the longest possible base length.
Edge cases: Either string may be empty only if permitted by constraints; mismatched repetition patterns fail the concatenation test.
Complexity: O(n+m) time and O(n+m) space for concatenation; the length GCD itself is O(log min(n,m)).
complexity_reason: Cross-concatenation equality tests a shared repeating pattern, while the length GCD selects its longest base.

title: Greatest Common Divisor of Strings
notes:
Task and constraints: Return the longest string that divides both input strings by repetition, or an empty string if none exists.
Idea: If `str1+str2` differs from `str2+str1`, return empty; otherwise the common repeating base has length `gcd(len(str1),len(str2))`.
Technique and why it applies: Cross-concatenation equality tests a shared repeating pattern, while the length GCD selects its longest base.
Invariant: Concatenation equality establishes that both strings are repetitions of the same base, and the length GCD gives the longest possible base length.
Edge cases: Either string may be empty only if permitted by constraints; mismatched repetition patterns fail the concatenation test.
Complexity: O(n+m) time and O(n+m) space for concatenation; the length GCD itself is O(log min(n,m)).
code: class Solution { public String gcdOfStrings(String a,String b){if(!(a+b).equals(b+a))return "";return a.substring(0,gcd(a.length(),b.length()));}private int gcd(int a,int b){while(b!=0){int t=a%b;a=b;b=t;}return a;} }
complexity_reason: Cross-concatenation equality tests a shared repeating pattern, while the length GCD selects its longest base.

title: Duplicate Zeros
notes:
Task and constraints: Modify an array in place so each zero is duplicated and elements beyond the original length are discarded.
Idea: Count how many zeros fit as duplicates within the fixed output boundary, then copy values backward so each zero occupies two positions when possible.
Technique and why it applies: Backward placement preserves unread elements while expanding zeros within the original array length.
Invariant: Backward copying prevents writes from overwriting values that have not yet been processed.
Edge cases: Zeros near the end may have only one copy retained; array length stays unchanged; elements beyond the original boundary are discarded.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space for the in-place approach.
complexity_reason: Backward placement preserves unread elements while expanding zeros within the original array length.

title: Duplicate Zeros
notes:
Task and constraints: Modify an array in place so each zero is duplicated and elements beyond the original length are discarded.
Idea: Count how many zeros fit as duplicates within the fixed output boundary, then copy values backward so each zero occupies two positions when possible.
Technique and why it applies: Backward placement preserves unread elements while expanding zeros within the original array length.
Invariant: Backward copying prevents writes from overwriting values that have not yet been processed.
Edge cases: Zeros near the end may have only one copy retained; array length stays unchanged; elements beyond the original boundary are discarded.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space for the in-place approach.
code: class Solution { public void duplicateZeros(int[] arr){int[]out=new int[arr.length];int j=0;for(int x:arr){if(j==out.length)break;out[j++]=x;if(x==0&&j<out.length)out[j++]=0;}System.arraycopy(out,0,arr,0,arr.length);} }
complexity_reason: Backward placement preserves unread elements while expanding zeros within the original array length.
